summary.summary: Brent's 2024/25 outturn shows external borrowing up £85.8m (10.5%) to £900.0m, funding a capital programme that pushed the Loan CFR up £102.6m to £1,357.1m (General Fund £1,015.1m, HRA £342.0m). A £13.7m budget variance on capital financing costs (£41.5m actual against a £27.8m budget) was offset by a drawdown from capital reserves. The council has grown related-party lending to its wholly-owned housing companies — £182.4m to I4B Holdings Ltd and £33.8m to First Wave Housing — and holds £59.5m of LOBO loans, of which £35.0m face an interest-rate review in 2025/26.

signals.headline: External borrowing rose £85.8m (10.5%) to £900.0m in 2024/25, from £170.0m of new loans against £84.2m of repayments.
signals.why: A rapid, double-digit rise in the debt stock within a single year.

signals.headline: A £13.7m capital-financing budget variance (£41.5m actual vs £27.8m budget) was offset by drawing down capital reserves.
signals.why: Financing costs are already outrunning budget, absorbed by reserves rather than a revised budget.

signals.headline: £35.0m of the council's £59.5m LOBO book (5 loans) is due an interest-rate review in 2025/26.
signals.why: If a lender exercises its option the council's own option is to repay at par, which is what councils do: every LOBO call we hold — Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, York, Barnet, Brighton and Hove, Bristol — was repaid rather than accepted. So the exposure is finding £35.0m and replacing that funding at today's rates, not paying a higher rate on it.

signals.headline: Loans to Brent's wholly-owned companies stood at £182.4m to I4B Holdings Ltd and £33.8m to First Wave Housing at 31 March 2025, both secured on company property, plus a £36.4m equity stake in I4B.
signals.why: Sizeable related-party credit exposure sits alongside the headline treasury debt figures.

news_drafts.headline: Brent's auditor not satisfied on value for money, citing two risks of significant weaknesses, in draft 2025-26 report
news_drafts.lead:
Grant Thornton, Brent's external auditor (the independent check on the council's accounts), says it has identified two risks of significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness. In its draft audit findings report for the Audit and Standards Advisory Committee on 23 September, it says it is therefore "not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements" for using its resources well. This is the auditor's value for money judgement, its separate view on whether the council manages its money and decision-making properly. Detailed findings are in a separate Auditor's Annual Report.

The accounts audit is not finished. The auditor cannot issue its certificate until an objection about council tax income recovered through enforcement action is resolved, though it says this has no material effect on the accounts. Confirmation from Danske Bank and management's calculations of borrowing interest costs are also awaited. The auditor says the cash audit was delayed because March 2026 bank reconciliations left out accounts shown in the trial balance. A query about cash in transit, first raised in July, stayed open until early September.

On the property figures, the auditor found land and buildings overstated by £7.3m and council dwellings understated by £6.5m, from incomplete indices used by the valuer across £914.8m of assets. Neither is material in 2025-26, but it says similar errors "could accumulate over successive years" and become so. Two assets worth £19.2m were reclassified from operational buildings to surplus assets. Assets carried at £10.4m should have had a desktop valuation in 2025-26 under the accounting code, but did not. Headteachers' pay of £461,000 was missing from last year's comparative figures and has been corrected.

The pension accounts show a net liability of £121.3m. The scheme has an underlying surplus of £94.4m, but the actuary found the council has no economic benefit available from it, an adjustment of £188.9m, and the council has £26.8m of unfunded obligations.

In the separate Pension Fund report, sales of investments were understated by £321.7m in the draft accounts. The corrected figures show investment value rising £148.5m, not falling £173.2m. Net assets were unaffected. A gap of 248 pensioner records between two systems has been reduced to 70, and a £3.2m cash-in-transit balance from an earlier system migration remains unreconciled.
news_drafts.paper_title: 10a. Appendix A - LB Brent Draft Audit Findings Report

news_drafts.headline: Brent auditor cannot sign off accounts or confirm proper financial management
news_drafts.lead: Brent Council's external auditor has been unable to formally conclude the 2025-26 accounts or issue an audit certificate, with outstanding matters including bank confirmations and pension calculations. The auditor has also identified two risks of significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements and is not satisfied it has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources, according to the draft audit findings report presented to the Audit and Standards Committee. The council did meet the statutory deadline for submitting draft accounts by 30 June and showed marked improvement in the quality of property valuation working papers, reversing substantial delays from previous years. However, audit delays across cash, financial instruments and debtors testing resulted in additional fees beyond the budgeted scale.

findings.headline: Care leavers placement cost avoidance (£110k) still in governance approval, six months after assumed implementation date
findings.detail: A £110k cost avoidance against care leavers' placements was included in Children's savings with an assumption of implementation from April 2026. As of Q2 (end September), this saving is still progressing through the governance approval process. The document flags this explicitly as a risk.
findings.matters: A saving assumed to land on 1 April has not cleared approval by end September. This signals either that the proposal was not governance-ready at budget time, or that approval processes are moving slowly. Both matter to council confidence in delivering budget assumptions on time.
findings.quote: The £110k cost avoidance against care leavers' placements was based on the assumption that the savings would be achieved and take effect from April 2026. However, these savings are still progressing through the governance approval process.

findings.headline: Asset Utilisation savings of £190k at risk due to delays in Padel Courts delivery model; delivery not expected in 2026/27
findings.detail: Asset Utilisation, a service-specific savings scheme under Neighbourhoods & Regeneration, is assessed as at risk (RAG Red). The document identifies delays in establishing the Padel Courts delivery model as the cause. More options to progress this are being put into action, but delivery in 2026-27 is not expected.
findings.matters: Signals a specific sports facility income scheme (Padel Courts) has slipped. Relevant to other councils considering similar leisure or sports income generation schemes and their realism. The Padel Courts model appears to be new, making it worth tracking whether leisure-facility-based income forecasts are surviving contact with delivery.
findings.quote: Asset Utilisation remaining at risk due to delays in establishing the Padel Courts delivery model

findings.headline: Digital Efficiency savings of £589k, £393k, £240k and £290k unidentified across four directorates with no implementation plans identified
findings.detail: Digital Efficiency savings are marked Red or Amber across Service Reform & Strategy (£589k unidentified), Neighbourhoods & Regeneration (£393k unidentified), Children's, and Residents & Housing. The pattern cited is implementation delays with no specific implementation plans identified to date. Councils are relying on mitigating actions identified under other savings themes (Commissioning, Workforce, Income Maximisation).
findings.matters: Suggests that across-the-board digital transformation savings targets are not materializing. This pattern is important to finance directors at other councils pursuing similar digital efficiency savings; it tests whether the sector is over-optimistic on digital returns.
findings.figures: Service Reform & Strategy £589,521 unidentified; Neighbourhoods & Regeneration £393,000 unidentified; Children's £290,000 variance; Residents & Housing £240,000 variance
findings.quote: The digital savings proposal is unlikely to be fully delivered at this stage. No implementation plans or specific areas for savings have been identified to date, creating a risk to achievement of the target within the required timeframe.

findings.headline: Children's Services £420k of £1.6m savings target unidentified, attributed to demand-led budget volatility
findings.detail: The council identified £1.18m savings against a £1.6m target for Children's Services, with £420k still unidentified at Q2. Digital Efficiency and Resident Experience savings proposals are noted as unlikely to be delivered, with no implementation plans identified to date. The document attributes the remaining shortfall to structural demand-led and volatile service pressures.
findings.matters: Children's Services is typically the most volatile element of a council budget; an unidentified £420k with five months left in the financial year signals either service overspend or need for rapid additional savings. Another council's finance director faces the same pressures and would be watching how Brent resolves this.
findings.figures: £1.18m identified of £1.6m target (£1.2m expected to be achieved); £420k unidentified
findings.quote: Savings delivery remains challenging, with around £1.2m of the £1.6m target expected to be achieved, while the remaining savings are subject to pressures arising from the demand-led and volatile nature of Children's Services budgets.

findings.headline: No breaches of Authorised Limit or Operational Boundary for external debt reported in Q1 2026/27
findings.detail: The Corporate Director for Finance and Resources confirms that the council remained in compliance with both its Authorised Limit (£2,000m for 2026/27) and Operational Boundary (£1,800m) throughout the first quarter of 2026/27. The council's actual external debt position (£1,223.2m including PFI and leases) remains well within both thresholds despite the large capital programme and rising borrowing levels.
findings.matters: The Authorised Limit and Operational Boundary are regulatory requirements under the Local Government Act 2003 and key management controls on debt. Compliance confirms the council is maintaining financial discipline despite significant new borrowing and investment activity.
findings.figures: Authorised Limit: £2,000m; Operational Boundary: £1,800m; actual total external debt liabilities: £1,223.2m (Q1 2026/27)
findings.quote: The Corporate Director for Finance and Resources confirms that there were no breaches to the Authorised Limit and the Operational Boundary during Quarter One of 2026/27.
